You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Earthquakes and seismically-induced landslides accelerate carbon export from mountains by eroding hillslope soil carbon. However, a quantitative understanding of their net contribution to carbon cycling remains incomplete. Using the 2008 Mw 7.9 Wenchuan Earthquake which generated the largest landslide volume in recent history, we quantify its carbon mass balance accounting for storage, loss, and transport within the ensuing sediment cascade. Thanks to post-event revegetation and extensive intermontane sediment storage, we show that the earthquake boosted Longmenshan carbon mass by ~10%. Given the stability of these deposits and low rates of carbon export, we anticipate this landslide carbon will persist for centuries to millennia before gradually declining. In effect, we demonstrate that earthquakes and landslides function as capacitors, regulating carbon storage and discharge across mountain belts over time. This suggests frequent landslides in seismically-active mountains may lead to a net carbon sequestration, providing a critical and direct link between tectonics and the carbon cycle.

---

## Introduction

Large earthquakes play a dual role in the terrestrial organic carbon system: they emit carbon to the atmosphere by destroying vegetation that subsequently decays, and they store particulate organic carbon in the ensuing sediment cascade. Landslides (hereafter explicitly coseismic) are the main players perturbing the carbon mass balance of a mountain belt during and following an earthquake. Organic carbon eroded by landslides can take a number of pathways through mountain catchments; some fraction is stored on hillslopes and in headwater channels, while the rest is exported via drainage networks and carried ultimately into long-term sinks. The amount of carbon temporarily stored in these landslide deposits, and the timescale over which it is released and exported, effectively act as a “carbon capacitor”, buffering the interval between carbon production and its eventual transfer downstream. While erosion of petrogenic (i.e., rock-derived) organic carbon also plays an important role in the long-term carbon cycle, our focus here is on the larger fluxes associated with production, burial, and loss of terrestrial organic carbon (hereafter explicitly OC) within mountain belts following large earthquakes.

The largest continental earthquakes generate up to ~50 km3 of landslide deposits composed of soil and fragmented rock. These earthquake-triggered slope failures entrain soil OC and live biomass, creating an OC store whose magnitude over time depends on the volume of landslide deposits and the rate at which they are eroded. Such deposits largely rest on hillslopes, where typically less than 10% are eroded immediately after the earthquake, while the majority remain stable for hundreds or even thousands of years. The rate of sediment and OC export is a function of the density of the newly developed drainage network on the landslide itself, together with its connectivity to the river below and the efficiency of hillslope erosion processes such as debris flows. Where this connectivity has been measured, for instance following the Chi-Chi, Wenchuan and Gorkha earthquakes, 5–60% of landslides are shown to be connected to a drainage network, though erosion is likely to be less efficient in the smallest headwater channels. The highest post-event sediment yields measured historically are reported from the 1970 Madang Earthquake (Papua New Guinea), where up to 50% of the mobilised sediment was exported in the first year. And yet, much lower yields are more typical, such as in the Matiri River (New Zealand), where at least 50–75% of the sediment generated by the 1929 Murchison Earthquake remained in the catchment 50 years later. Evacuation of the 1999 Chi-Chi Earthquake debris filling the Peikang River is predicted to take centuries, just as 70% still remains intact of the 5–7 km3 of sediment injected into the Pokhara Valley (Nepal) by medieval earthquakes.

In line with sediment flux, OC export from seismically active mountain belts varies widely: 0.12–0.28 teragrams (TgC) per year following the Gorkha Earthquake and up to 35–40 TgC per year to the offshore of Taiwan, while a sediment record from Lake Paringa indicates that 14±5 TgC was eroded during a single earthquake on New Zealand’s Alpine Fault. Nevertheless, existing research on post-earthquake carbon dynamics has tended to focus on sediment fluxes and revegetation, whereas the role of transient OC storage held within landslides has been overlooked. We propose that the observed worldwide variation in carbon export reflects either (1) differences in the primary mass of OC mobilised during an earthquake, or (2) the potential for landslides to function as transient stores (a “capacitor effect”) that mediate the release of sediment and OC beyond the mountain belt. These two hypotheses serve as the focus for our study.

The 2008 Mw 7.9 Wenchuan Earthquake is a large historical landslide event of between 3 and 15 km3 (6000–30,000 Tg of sediment, assuming an average density of landslide deposits of 2000 kg/m3) of erosion. Thanks to the intensive study of the resultant sediment cascade, Wenchuan is one of the best understood examples of post-earthquake erosional response. The earthquake struck at a time of rapid expansion of satellite technologies, which have allowed researchers to constrain the frequency and intensity of landsliding, the reworking of sediment from landslides into the drainage network, and the changes in vegetation coverage after the event. As the largest earthquake-triggered landsliding event of the past 50 years, the Wenchuan example provides a unique opportunity to understand the carbon dynamics at scale. Our analysis therefore aims to constrain the potential upper bound of landslide-driven carbon storage and transient carbon transfer in mountain systems, rather than to represent the average behaviour across all earthquakes. Well-established river gauging in the affected region revealed a doubling of particulate OC transport via streams in the Zagunao catchment in the first four years, but the post-earthquake analysis remains incomplete. Here, we present a comprehensive OC budget for the period, 2008–2020, by integrating fieldwork, laboratory analyses, remote sensing and numerical modelling. Mapping of carbon stocks pre- and post-earthquake allows us to quantify the hillslope carbon mass balance for this earthquake with unprecedented precision. This framework further enables us to assess the long-term trajectory of carbon storage within mountainous landscapes.

---

## Results

Spatial distribution of carbon and its erosion by landslides
We set out to identify and measure carbon stocks directly in the field at 123 sites comprising landslide deposits and areas undisturbed by earthquakes across the Longmenshan study area. These field data are augmented with data extracted from previous studies. A subset of our dataset, scored for high quality, was incorporated into a machine-learning model that aims to simulate retrodictively the spatial distribution of carbon stocks prior to the Wenchuan Earthquake based on a wider range of parameters (Table S1) (see Methods).

Prior to the Wenchuan Earthquake, we estimate the average OC stock across the Longmenshan study area at 136±25 megagrams carbon per hectare (Mg C ha–1), an average that embraces local variability of 50–260 Mg C ha–1 (note that all uncertainties are given as ±1 standard deviation, unless otherwise stated; units for carbon stock are presented as Mg C ha–1 and carbon flux is expressed as Mg C km2 yr–1). The spatial distribution of pre-earthquake OC stock correlates with topography and climate. The OC (within surface soil and vegetation) increases with elevation between 500–2000 metres above sea level (masl) but varies little outside that range (Figs. S1, S2). The highest concentration of total OC is found on the steepest mountains close to the range front where average precipitation rates are also highest (Fig. 1A, B).

Wenchuan landslides eroded 5.5±0.01 Tg C, amounting to 2–6 weight percent (wt%) of global annual terrestrial carbon erosion. The spatial distribution of landsliding relates to topography, lithology, and position relative to the fault rupture, and the majority (2.5±0.6 km3) of the landslide volume occurred within the Minjiang and Tuojiang basins (Fig. 1B). Corresponding erosion of OC by landslides in these two catchments equalled 4.5±0.01 Tg C, which accounts for 82±0.2% of the overall OC denuded by landslides associated with this event. The large OC stock in the Fujiang catchment remained largely intact, consistent with the spatial distribution of pre- and post-earthquake net primary production (NPP), which saw little change over this area (Fig. S3). These eroded OC are rapidly mobilised and widely deposited along hillslopes and channels, awaiting further transport or transformation.

Recovery of carbon stocks following landslides
A decade after the Wenchuan Earthquake, landslides stored 33±21 Mg C ha–1 of OC in the study area (Fig. 2B). The recovery rate (i.e., growth) of OC was 475±110 Mg C km–2 yr–1 on landslide surfaces and 5.5±0.02 Mg C km–2 yr–1 when applied to the overall affected area, reflecting that landslides account for only about 8% of the total landscape area. The major components of the OC storage at these sites were soil OC (55±29%) and tree biomass (32±29%) (Fig. S4). Soil OC content is positively correlated with total soil nitrogen content (TN) for all sites (Fig. S5). New vegetation on landslide surfaces (including both deposit and scar areas) accounts for a quarter of the pre-earthquake OC stock (Fig. S6). Recovery was characterised by a major change in the species composition from a pre-earthquake community of Pinus tabuliformis, Cupressus funerbri and Cryptomeria fortunei to a recovery community of Alnus cremastogyne, Populus alba and Ziziphus jujuba (Fig. S7).

Vegetation coverage on landslide surfaces had recovered to 80–90% of pre-earthquake levels within a decade, as inferred from metrics including normalised difference vegetation index, enhanced vegetation index, leaf area index. This observation is consistent with time series of net primary productivity (NPP) changes in our study area (Fig. 2B). Here, NPP was used solely to assess the temporal recovery of vegetation productivity, not as a direct measure of total carbon storage. NPP of both the whole landscape and landslide areas decreased immediately after the earthquake from 760±110 Mg C km–2 yr–1 (in 2007) to a low point of 580±120 Mg C km–2 yr–1 (in 2010), after which NPP recovered rapidly and reached pre-earthquake levels around 2015. Despite the rapid increase in NPP during this initial stage of recovery, total carbon storage within the landscape remained deficient due to the slower return of soil carbon and vegetation biomass (Fig. 2). Landslide surfaces sequestered 3.5±0.01 Tg C via NPP, referring to the amount of OC fixed by plant photosynthesis minus losses from plant respiration. The upscaled OC, derived from field-measured OC, for landslide surfaces is 2.2±0.01 Tg C, which is much smaller than the pre-earthquake level of 5.5±0.01 Tg C. The field-measured OC represents the combined carbon storage in soil and vegetation biomass. The measured OC was about 10% lower than the NPP-derived estimate, which could partly reflect measurement uncertainty, in addition to potential carbon loss via fluvial transport, decomposition, and soil respiration.

Hillslope carbon budget after an earthquake
Using our estimates of burial and recovery of OC after the Wenchuan Earthquake, we calculated the hillslope carbon budget for the decade after the earthquake (Table S2). We determined the total volume of carbon stored in landslides (Fig. 3) based on the sediment export flux to the fluvial system from prior work, together with our results showing that pre-earthquake soil and vegetation OC are well mixed in landslide deposits—allowing us to assume that the proportional removal of OC is similar to that of sediment. On this basis, we estimate that 12% of the carbon stored in landslide deposits has been evacuated, primarily by debris flows. The OC yield implied in this calculation falls within the uncertainty range of field measurements from the Zagunao catchment in the study area. As an upper bound for erosion, we can also assume that all of the material in landslide deposits that are connected to the fluvial network has been evacuated, resulting in the removal of 43% of carbon mobilised by landslides. Considering this range, hillslope landslide deposits apparently retained between 3.1 and 4.8 Tg C of the mass that was previously held in soils and vegetation. Based on field observations and the detailed sediment budget for this event, storage is likely to be closer to the upper bound of 4.8 Tg C. Meanwhile, 2.2±0.01 Tg C was restored on the hillslopes. Overall, the Wenchuan Earthquake has stored up to 7.0 Tg C within landslide-affected areas between 2008 and 2020 (Fig. 3).

---

## Methods

Sampling sites
Our study area covers 33,005 km2 of the region most severely affected by the 2008 Mw 7.9 Wenchuan Earthquake. Landslides occurred primarily in mountainous terrain within four large river systems: the Minjiang, Tuojiang, Fujiang and Bailongjiang (Fig. S8). We selected 123 sampling sites for field investigation, of which 59 were on coseismic landslide deposits (disturbed sites) and 64 were on adjacent undisturbed areas with no clear slope failure (since 2008) based on aerial and satellite imagery. The disturbed sites were randomly distributed along the major faults of the Longmenshan that ruptured during the earthquake.

Plot design
The plot design for sampling followed previous studies in the Luoquanwan catchment. Measured OC is composed of soil, tree, understorey plant and litter OC. The simplified vegetation OC represents the tree, understorey plant and litter OC. Within a 5-m radius plot (after slope correction), all trees with a diameter at breast height (DBH) >5 cm were recorded for species, DBH and total height (Table S2). Heights of trees were measured in each plot using a Vertex III height meter (Haglöf, Sweden). Plants with DBH <5 cm were considered as understorey. To estimate biomass of the understorey and litter, three 1-m radius circular subplots were set at three directions (0°, 120°, 240°, 3 m from the plot centre) within the 5-m radius plots. Understorey and litter within each subplot were dried and weighed. Within the three subplots, soil samples were collected in cloth bags down to 50 cm in three layers: 0–10 cm, 10–30 cm, and 30–50 cm, respectively. Soil samples from the same layer were mixed for each given sub-plot location. Soil samples were collected using standard ring cores with a diameter of 70 cm for each layer to analyse soil physical properties in undisturbed areas. Due to the high gravel content of landslide deposits, a circular bucket with fixed volume was used to obtain the wet density for different layers. A detailed list of collected samples is shown in Table S4.

Landslide inventory
We used a published landslide inventory to calculate the total carbon budget. This dataset covers over 90% of the surface rupture area and the zones of most concentrated landslide density. The approach for constructing the carbon budget is described in detail in the Supplementary Information. Estimates of carbon storage in coseismic landslides include only failures >5800 m2, consistent with the 30×30 m resolution of the prediction model described in the method of modelling of carbon stock. Landslides >10,000 m2 were selected for field sampling as they were easily recognized from satellite images. The mass of total OC, as determined through gridded data, is presented in Table S3 pre-earthquake, along with the mobilisation and recovery post-earthquake.

Landslide volume and area
To model the carbon balance following the 2008 Wenchuan Earthquake, it is essential to estimate landslide volumes, which directly determine the timescale of sediment and carbon transport. We used a common approach of applying a power-law volume-area relationship to convert the landslide inventory to landslide volumes. There is significant uncertainty with this approach, but the satellite imagery available to us precludes a more accurate volume-based approach. Instead, we use a range of different area-volume scaling parameters and scar-deposit correction methods, as detailed in Supplementary Information. None of the available landslide inventories distinguishes between landslide types or between source and deposit areas making direct inferences about volume a challenge. Here we have compared different approaches to estimate the potential range of volume uncertainty (Tables S11 S12).

Soil physical properties, organic carbon and total nitrogen
All soil samples were dried in an oven at 85°C to a constant weight. Bulk density, water content, and gravel fraction (>2 mm) were analysed following standard methods. For the disturbed sites, wet density was measured in the field. Identifiable plant residues and roots were removed manually, and samples were sieved at 0.15, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, and 5.0 mm intervals. Soil OC content was analysed using the potassium dichromate and sulphuric acid (K2Cr2O7–H2SO4) wet oxidation method. Total nitrogen (TN) content was determined by the automatic Kjeldahl apparatus method following the Chinese Agriculture Industry Standard (NY/T1121.24-2012). Both soil OC and TN analyses were repeated three times for each sample.

Vegetation biomass calculation
Tree biomass was calculated using a dataset of Chinese allometric equations. We estimated above-ground and below-ground biomass by selecting the appropriate allometric relationship based on the tree species, diameter and height range, mean annual precipitation (MAP), mean annual temperature (MAT), and location. For species not found in the database, we applied the general allometry by plant functional group (e.g., deciduous broad-leaved forest or evergreen broad-leaved forest). We included all major biomass components, including stem, branch, leaf, and below-ground biomass. Tree species and related allometric models are given in Table S5. All sampled understorey vegetation and litter samples within three 1-m radius circular subplots were dried at 70°C to a constant weight. Carbon content of 0.5 g g–1 was used to convert biomass to C stock.

Soil OC stock
The soil organic C stock (Mg ha–1) for each layer was calculated using the following formula:

SOCstock = SOC × BD × (1 – RC) × D / 10

where total SOC stock (Mg C ha–1) is the soil OC concentration (g kg–1); BD is bulk density (g cm–3); RC is gravel (>2 mm) content; D is soil layer depth (cm).

Data compiled from previous studies
We compiled previously published OC data from the study area (194 entries derived from 25 publications), focusing on studies that report field sampling data in undisturbed forest and shrub ecosystems, excluding those based on models or satellite data, as well as planted forests. For inclusion data must include geographical coordinates, and at least one of the following: soil organic carbon, above-ground and below-ground biomass, or total carbon (see Fig. S9). Data quality was evaluated by assigning scores, 0–2, based on eight categories (namely data type, data information, climate information, geographic information, soil information, soil organic carbon, vegetation organic carbon and total terrestrial organic carbon), with the maximum cumulative score being 16 (see Table S6). This dataset will serve as a reference for further research conducted in the Longmenshan Range or the Tibetan Plateau (see Source Data 1).

For the training of the machine-learning predictive model, we utilized previous study datasets scoring >5, together with our own field-measured dataset. Soil C stock was normalised to a depth of 50 cm; for soil profiles <50 cm, extrapolation was performed by averaging the C content and dry bulk density from known depths and then applying it to 50 cm. The augmented data helps to overcome the spatial limitations inherent in our field-measured dataset.

Modelling of carbon stock
During preliminary screening, we trialled twenty different predictive models to identify the most suitable for total OC stock; these included: random forest, gradient boosting decision trees (GBDT), extreme gradient boost, decision tree, support vector regression, k-nearest neighbour regression, linear weight regression, etc. Twenty covariates derived from remote sensing data, geographic data and landslide inventory were applied. The prediction models were built using representative topographic and soil characteristics, climatic, and vegetation indices across the study area, and include landslide area, slope, aspect, elevation, lithology, MAP, MAT, land surface temperature, TN, clay content, bulk density, Landsat derived enhanced vegetation index, normalised difference vegetation index, red band and modified soil adjusted vegetation index, MODIS product (MOD17A3) derived enhance vegetation index, normalized difference vegetation, red band and modified soil adjusted vegetation index and gross primary production, as specified in Table S1. The raster maps of these variables were resampled to 10 m resolution for spatial calculation, consistent with DEM resolution.

To ensure that our model was applied only to forest ecosystems, we used the 30 m Landsat-derived annual land-cover dataset for China to define land use types (with categories: forest, shrub, grassland, wetland, farmland, urban and other), and areas not identified as forest or shrub were excluded.

We trained the machine-learning prediction model using the total carbon stock data from our field-measured data and the twenty covariates noted above. We developed models for disturbed and undisturbed sites trained using 70% of the field sampling data, leaving the remaining 30% for testing. After training and testing, we found that the GBDT method was the best performer (see Table S7). Figure S10 presents the importance of covariates within the training samples as identified by the GBDT.

Modelling of carbon balance
To quantify the temporal trend of major carbon pools under the impact of the 2008 Wenchuan Earthquake, our carbon balance model adopts a pool–flux structure, employing a set of differential equations to simplify the connection between carbon flux and mass movements. We derived the parameters for the carbon balance model by integrating subsequent research and data collected since the Wenchuan event (particularly the carbon stock distribution maps obtained from empirical data noted above). This approach ensures that the parameter settings are tailored to our study area and effectively reflect complex environmental interactions. The carbon balance modelling separates into three main parts: constructing the carbon balance framework, introducing earthquake-triggered landslides and implementing carbon balance model. The model is based on two key assumptions: (1) following the earthquake, the entire aboveground biomass carbon pool (B) is converted into debris (D) that is fully mixed with soil carbon and buried within landslide deposits. Because this exact initial B–D portioning lacks empirical constraint, it represents a source of uncertainty in the estimated long-term carbon storage. This assumption represents an endmember maximum potential carbon storage after the earthquake; (2) ecosystems outside the landslide surface areas are assumed to have remained undisturbed, regions showing no bare surfaces or vegetation loss are assumed to have the same stock before and after the earthquake. The major carbon pools and fluxes are shown in Fig. S11.

Statistical analyses
For our field data, descriptive statistical analyses were conducted to characterise the spatial variations of soil organic carbon (SOC) content, soil total nitrogen (TN) content, and soil OC stock with depth, as well as tree, understory, litter, and total ecosystem organic carbon stocks in both undisturbed areas and landslide deposits (Table S8). Prior to model training, multicollinearity among covariates was evaluated using Pearson correlation analysis (Fig. S12). For the modelling of carbon stock analysis, we applied the Shapiro–Wilk test to examine the representativeness and normality of twenty selected covariates (see Table S9). Subsequently, a one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA, F test) was used to test whether the effect of coseismic landslides on OC stock is distinguishable (p<0.05) when comparing undisturbed areas and landslide deposits (see Table S10).

Data availability
The data generated or analysed during this study are included in the paper, Supplementary Information and the Source Data 1. Source data are provided with this paper.

Code availability
The codes to produce the carbon balance model are available at https://github.com/liujie1408/carbon-dynamics-model

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications.

You previously reviewed this paper and raised several concerns. The authors have now submitted a revised manuscript along with a detailed point-by-point response. Your task is to write your updated review after carefully reading:
  1. The revised paper
  2. Your original Round 1 review
  3. The authors' point-by-point response

In your updated review, explicitly state which concerns have been adequately addressed and which remain outstanding. Be specific.

## Paper

## Abstract

Earthquakes and seismically-induced landslides accelerate carbon export from mountains by eroding hillslope soil carbon. However, a quantitative understanding of their net contribution to carbon cycling remains incomplete. Using the 2008 Mw 7.9 Wenchuan Earthquake which generated the largest landslide volume in recent history, we quantify its carbon mass balance accounting for storage, loss, and transport within the ensuing sediment cascade. Thanks to post-event revegetation and extensive intermontane sediment storage, we show that the earthquake boosted Longmenshan carbon mass by ~10%. Given the stability of these deposits and low rates of carbon export, we anticipate this landslide carbon will persist for centuries to millennia before gradually declining. In effect, we demonstrate that earthquakes and landslides function as capacitors, regulating carbon storage and discharge across mountain belts over time. This suggests frequent landslides in seismically-active mountains may lead to a net carbon sequestration, providing a critical and direct link between tectonics and the carbon cycle.

---

## Introduction

Large earthquakes play a dual role in the terrestrial organic carbon system: they emit carbon to the atmosphere by destroying vegetation that subsequently decays, and they store particulate organic carbon in the ensuing sediment cascade. Landslides (hereafter explicitly coseismic) are the main players perturbing the carbon mass balance of a mountain belt during and following an earthquake. Organic carbon eroded by landslides can take a number of pathways through mountain catchments; some fraction is stored on hillslopes and in headwater channels, while the rest is exported via drainage networks and carried ultimately into long-term sinks. The amount of carbon temporarily stored in these landslide deposits, and the timescale over which it is released and exported, effectively act as a “carbon capacitor”, buffering the interval between carbon production and its eventual transfer downstream. While erosion of petrogenic (i.e., rock-derived) organic carbon also plays an important role in the long-term carbon cycle, our focus here is on the larger fluxes associated with production, burial, and loss of terrestrial organic carbon (hereafter explicitly OC) within mountain belts following large earthquakes.

The largest continental earthquakes generate up to ~50 km3 of landslide deposits composed of soil and fragmented rock. These earthquake-triggered slope failures entrain soil OC and live biomass, creating an OC store whose magnitude over time depends on the volume of landslide deposits and the rate at which they are eroded. Such deposits largely rest on hillslopes, where typically less than 10% are eroded immediately after the earthquake, while the majority remain stable for hundreds or even thousands of years. The rate of sediment and OC export is a function of the density of the newly developed drainage network on the landslide itself, together with its connectivity to the river below and the efficiency of hillslope erosion processes such as debris flows. Where this connectivity has been measured, for instance following the Chi-Chi, Wenchuan and Gorkha earthquakes, 5–60% of landslides are shown to be connected to a drainage network, though erosion is likely to be less efficient in the smallest headwater channels. The highest post-event sediment yields measured historically are reported from the 1970 Madang Earthquake (Papua New Guinea), where up to 50% of the mobilised sediment was exported in the first year. And yet, much lower yields are more typical, such as in the Matiri River (New Zealand), where at least 50–75% of the sediment generated by the 1929 Murchison Earthquake remained in the catchment 50 years later. Evacuation of the 1999 Chi-Chi Earthquake debris filling the Peikang River is predicted to take centuries, just as 70% still remains intact of the 5–7 km3 of sediment injected into the Pokhara Valley (Nepal) by medieval earthquakes.

In line with sediment flux, OC export from seismically active mountain belts varies widely: 0.12–0.28 teragrams (TgC) per year following the Gorkha Earthquake and up to 35–40 TgC per year to the offshore of Taiwan, while a sediment record from Lake Paringa indicates that 14±5 TgC was eroded during a single earthquake on New Zealand’s Alpine Fault. Nevertheless, existing research on post-earthquake carbon dynamics has tended to focus on sediment fluxes and revegetation, whereas the role of transient OC storage held within landslides has been overlooked. We propose that the observed worldwide variation in carbon export reflects either (1) differences in the primary mass of OC mobilised during an earthquake, or (2) the potential for landslides to function as transient stores (a “capacitor effect”) that mediate the release of sediment and OC beyond the mountain belt. These two hypotheses serve as the focus for our study.

The 2008 Mw 7.9 Wenchuan Earthquake is a large historical landslide event of between 3 and 15 km3 (6000–30,000 Tg of sediment, assuming an average density of landslide deposits of 2000 kg/m3) of erosion. Thanks to the intensive study of the resultant sediment cascade, Wenchuan is one of the best understood examples of post-earthquake erosional response. The earthquake struck at a time of rapid expansion of satellite technologies, which have allowed researchers to constrain the frequency and intensity of landsliding, the reworking of sediment from landslides into the drainage network, and the changes in vegetation coverage after the event. As the largest earthquake-triggered landsliding event of the past 50 years, the Wenchuan example provides a unique opportunity to understand the carbon dynamics at scale. Our analysis therefore aims to constrain the potential upper bound of landslide-driven carbon storage and transient carbon transfer in mountain systems, rather than to represent the average behaviour across all earthquakes. Well-established river gauging in the affected region revealed a doubling of particulate OC transport via streams in the Zagunao catchment in the first four years, but the post-earthquake analysis remains incomplete. Here, we present a comprehensive OC budget for the period, 2008–2020, by integrating fieldwork, laboratory analyses, remote sensing and numerical modelling. Mapping of carbon stocks pre- and post-earthquake allows us to quantify the hillslope carbon mass balance for this earthquake with unprecedented precision. This framework further enables us to assess the long-term trajectory of carbon storage within mountainous landscapes.

---

## Results

Spatial distribution of carbon and its erosion by landslides
We set out to identify and measure carbon stocks directly in the field at 123 sites comprising landslide deposits and areas undisturbed by earthquakes across the Longmenshan study area. These field data are augmented with data extracted from previous studies. A subset of our dataset, scored for high quality, was incorporated into a machine-learning model that aims to simulate retrodictively the spatial distribution of carbon stocks prior to the Wenchuan Earthquake based on a wider range of parameters (Table S1) (see Methods).

Prior to the Wenchuan Earthquake, we estimate the average OC stock across the Longmenshan study area at 136±25 megagrams carbon per hectare (Mg C ha–1), an average that embraces local variability of 50–260 Mg C ha–1 (note that all uncertainties are given as ±1 standard deviation, unless otherwise stated; units for carbon stock are presented as Mg C ha–1 and carbon flux is expressed as Mg C km2 yr–1). The spatial distribution of pre-earthquake OC stock correlates with topography and climate. The OC (within surface soil and vegetation) increases with elevation between 500–2000 metres above sea level (masl) but varies little outside that range (Figs. S1, S2). The highest concentration of total OC is found on the steepest mountains close to the range front where average precipitation rates are also highest (Fig. 1A, B).

Wenchuan landslides eroded 5.5±0.01 Tg C, amounting to 2–6 weight percent (wt%) of global annual terrestrial carbon erosion. The spatial distribution of landsliding relates to topography, lithology, and position relative to the fault rupture, and the majority (2.5±0.6 km3) of the landslide volume occurred within the Minjiang and Tuojiang basins (Fig. 1B). Corresponding erosion of OC by landslides in these two catchments equalled 4.5±0.01 Tg C, which accounts for 82±0.2% of the overall OC denuded by landslides associated with this event. The large OC stock in the Fujiang catchment remained largely intact, consistent with the spatial distribution of pre- and post-earthquake net primary production (NPP), which saw little change over this area (Fig. S3). These eroded OC are rapidly mobilised and widely deposited along hillslopes and channels, awaiting further transport or transformation.

Recovery of carbon stocks following landslides
A decade after the Wenchuan Earthquake, landslides stored 33±21 Mg C ha–1 of OC in the study area (Fig. 2B). The recovery rate (i.e., growth) of OC was 475±110 Mg C km–2 yr–1 on landslide surfaces and 5.5±0.02 Mg C km–2 yr–1 when applied to the overall affected area, reflecting that landslides account for only about 8% of the total landscape area. The major components of the OC storage at these sites were soil OC (55±29%) and tree biomass (32±29%) (Fig. S4). Soil OC content is positively correlated with total soil nitrogen content (TN) for all sites (Fig. S5). New vegetation on landslide surfaces (including both deposit and scar areas) accounts for a quarter of the pre-earthquake OC stock (Fig. S6). Recovery was characterised by a major change in the species composition from a pre-earthquake community of Pinus tabuliformis, Cupressus funerbri and Cryptomeria fortunei to a recovery community of Alnus cremastogyne, Populus alba and Ziziphus jujuba (Fig. S7).

Vegetation coverage on landslide surfaces had recovered to 80–90% of pre-earthquake levels within a decade, as inferred from metrics including normalised difference vegetation index, enhanced vegetation index, leaf area index. This observation is consistent with time series of net primary productivity (NPP) changes in our study area (Fig. 2B). Here, NPP was used solely to assess the temporal recovery of vegetation productivity, not as a direct measure of total carbon storage. NPP of both the whole landscape and landslide areas decreased immediately after the earthquake from 760±110 Mg C km–2 yr–1 (in 2007) to a low point of 580±120 Mg C km–2 yr–1 (in 2010), after which NPP recovered rapidly and reached pre-earthquake levels around 2015. Despite the rapid increase in NPP during this initial stage of recovery, total carbon storage within the landscape remained deficient due to the slower return of soil carbon and vegetation biomass (Fig. 2). Landslide surfaces sequestered 3.5±0.01 Tg C via NPP, referring to the amount of OC fixed by plant photosynthesis minus losses from plant respiration. The upscaled OC, derived from field-measured OC, for landslide surfaces is 2.2±0.01 Tg C, which is much smaller than the pre-earthquake level of 5.5±0.01 Tg C. The field-measured OC represents the combined carbon storage in soil and vegetation biomass. The measured OC was about 10% lower than the NPP-derived estimate, which could partly reflect measurement uncertainty, in addition to potential carbon loss via fluvial transport, decomposition, and soil respiration.

Hillslope carbon budget after an earthquake
Using our estimates of burial and recovery of OC after the Wenchuan Earthquake, we calculated the hillslope carbon budget for the decade after the earthquake (Table S2). We determined the total volume of carbon stored in landslides (Fig. 3) based on the sediment export flux to the fluvial system from prior work, together with our results showing that pre-earthquake soil and vegetation OC are well mixed in landslide deposits—allowing us to assume that the proportional removal of OC is similar to that of sediment. On this basis, we estimate that 12% of the carbon stored in landslide deposits has been evacuated, primarily by debris flows. The OC yield implied in this calculation falls within the uncertainty range of field measurements from the Zagunao catchment in the study area. As an upper bound for erosion, we can also assume that all of the material in landslide deposits that are connected to the fluvial network has been evacuated, resulting in the removal of 43% of carbon mobilised by landslides. Considering this range, hillslope landslide deposits apparently retained between 3.1 and 4.8 Tg C of the mass that was previously held in soils and vegetation. Based on field observations and the detailed sediment budget for this event, storage is likely to be closer to the upper bound of 4.8 Tg C. Meanwhile, 2.2±0.01 Tg C was restored on the hillslopes. Overall, the Wenchuan Earthquake has stored up to 7.0 Tg C within landslide-affected areas between 2008 and 2020 (Fig. 3).

---

## Methods

Sampling sites
Our study area covers 33,005 km2 of the region most severely affected by the 2008 Mw 7.9 Wenchuan Earthquake. Landslides occurred primarily in mountainous terrain within four large river systems: the Minjiang, Tuojiang, Fujiang and Bailongjiang (Fig. S8). We selected 123 sampling sites for field investigation, of which 59 were on coseismic landslide deposits (disturbed sites) and 64 were on adjacent undisturbed areas with no clear slope failure (since 2008) based on aerial and satellite imagery. The disturbed sites were randomly distributed along the major faults of the Longmenshan that ruptured during the earthquake.

Plot design
The plot design for sampling followed previous studies in the Luoquanwan catchment. Measured OC is composed of soil, tree, understorey plant and litter OC. The simplified vegetation OC represents the tree, understorey plant and litter OC. Within a 5-m radius plot (after slope correction), all trees with a diameter at breast height (DBH) >5 cm were recorded for species, DBH and total height (Table S2). Heights of trees were measured in each plot using a Vertex III height meter (Haglöf, Sweden). Plants with DBH <5 cm were considered as understorey. To estimate biomass of the understorey and litter, three 1-m radius circular subplots were set at three directions (0°, 120°, 240°, 3 m from the plot centre) within the 5-m radius plots. Understorey and litter within each subplot were dried and weighed. Within the three subplots, soil samples were collected in cloth bags down to 50 cm in three layers: 0–10 cm, 10–30 cm, and 30–50 cm, respectively. Soil samples from the same layer were mixed for each given sub-plot location. Soil samples were collected using standard ring cores with a diameter of 70 cm for each layer to analyse soil physical properties in undisturbed areas. Due to the high gravel content of landslide deposits, a circular bucket with fixed volume was used to obtain the wet density for different layers. A detailed list of collected samples is shown in Table S4.

Landslide inventory
We used a published landslide inventory to calculate the total carbon budget. This dataset covers over 90% of the surface rupture area and the zones of most concentrated landslide density. The approach for constructing the carbon budget is described in detail in the Supplementary Information. Estimates of carbon storage in coseismic landslides include only failures >5800 m2, consistent with the 30×30 m resolution of the prediction model described in the method of modelling of carbon stock. Landslides >10,000 m2 were selected for field sampling as they were easily recognized from satellite images. The mass of total OC, as determined through gridded data, is presented in Table S3 pre-earthquake, along with the mobilisation and recovery post-earthquake.

Landslide volume and area
To model the carbon balance following the 2008 Wenchuan Earthquake, it is essential to estimate landslide volumes, which directly determine the timescale of sediment and carbon transport. We used a common approach of applying a power-law volume-area relationship to convert the landslide inventory to landslide volumes. There is significant uncertainty with this approach, but the satellite imagery available to us precludes a more accurate volume-based approach. Instead, we use a range of different area-volume scaling parameters and scar-deposit correction methods, as detailed in Supplementary Information. None of the available landslide inventories distinguishes between landslide types or between source and deposit areas making direct inferences about volume a challenge. Here we have compared different approaches to estimate the potential range of volume uncertainty (Tables S11 S12).

Soil physical properties, organic carbon and total nitrogen
All soil samples were dried in an oven at 85°C to a constant weight. Bulk density, water content, and gravel fraction (>2 mm) were analysed following standard methods. For the disturbed sites, wet density was measured in the field. Identifiable plant residues and roots were removed manually, and samples were sieved at 0.15, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, and 5.0 mm intervals. Soil OC content was analysed using the potassium dichromate and sulphuric acid (K2Cr2O7–H2SO4) wet oxidation method. Total nitrogen (TN) content was determined by the automatic Kjeldahl apparatus method following the Chinese Agriculture Industry Standard (NY/T1121.24-2012). Both soil OC and TN analyses were repeated three times for each sample.

Vegetation biomass calculation
Tree biomass was calculated using a dataset of Chinese allometric equations. We estimated above-ground and below-ground biomass by selecting the appropriate allometric relationship based on the tree species, diameter and height range, mean annual precipitation (MAP), mean annual temperature (MAT), and location. For species not found in the database, we applied the general allometry by plant functional group (e.g., deciduous broad-leaved forest or evergreen broad-leaved forest). We included all major biomass components, including stem, branch, leaf, and below-ground biomass. Tree species and related allometric models are given in Table S5. All sampled understorey vegetation and litter samples within three 1-m radius circular subplots were dried at 70°C to a constant weight. Carbon content of 0.5 g g–1 was used to convert biomass to C stock.

Soil OC stock
The soil organic C stock (Mg ha–1) for each layer was calculated using the following formula:

SOCstock = SOC × BD × (1 – RC) × D / 10

where total SOC stock (Mg C ha–1) is the soil OC concentration (g kg–1); BD is bulk density (g cm–3); RC is gravel (>2 mm) content; D is soil layer depth (cm).

Data compiled from previous studies
We compiled previously published OC data from the study area (194 entries derived from 25 publications), focusing on studies that report field sampling data in undisturbed forest and shrub ecosystems, excluding those based on models or satellite data, as well as planted forests. For inclusion data must include geographical coordinates, and at least one of the following: soil organic carbon, above-ground and below-ground biomass, or total carbon (see Fig. S9). Data quality was evaluated by assigning scores, 0–2, based on eight categories (namely data type, data information, climate information, geographic information, soil information, soil organic carbon, vegetation organic carbon and total terrestrial organic carbon), with the maximum cumulative score being 16 (see Table S6). This dataset will serve as a reference for further research conducted in the Longmenshan Range or the Tibetan Plateau (see Source Data 1).

For the training of the machine-learning predictive model, we utilized previous study datasets scoring >5, together with our own field-measured dataset. Soil C stock was normalised to a depth of 50 cm; for soil profiles <50 cm, extrapolation was performed by averaging the C content and dry bulk density from known depths and then applying it to 50 cm. The augmented data helps to overcome the spatial limitations inherent in our field-measured dataset.

Modelling of carbon stock
During preliminary screening, we trialled twenty different predictive models to identify the most suitable for total OC stock; these included: random forest, gradient boosting decision trees (GBDT), extreme gradient boost, decision tree, support vector regression, k-nearest neighbour regression, linear weight regression, etc. Twenty covariates derived from remote sensing data, geographic data and landslide inventory were applied. The prediction models were built using representative topographic and soil characteristics, climatic, and vegetation indices across the study area, and include landslide area, slope, aspect, elevation, lithology, MAP, MAT, land surface temperature, TN, clay content, bulk density, Landsat derived enhanced vegetation index, normalised difference vegetation index, red band and modified soil adjusted vegetation index, MODIS product (MOD17A3) derived enhance vegetation index, normalized difference vegetation, red band and modified soil adjusted vegetation index and gross primary production, as specified in Table S1. The raster maps of these variables were resampled to 10 m resolution for spatial calculation, consistent with DEM resolution.

To ensure that our model was applied only to forest ecosystems, we used the 30 m Landsat-derived annual land-cover dataset for China to define land use types (with categories: forest, shrub, grassland, wetland, farmland, urban and other), and areas not identified as forest or shrub were excluded.

We trained the machine-learning prediction model using the total carbon stock data from our field-measured data and the twenty covariates noted above. We developed models for disturbed and undisturbed sites trained using 70% of the field sampling data, leaving the remaining 30% for testing. After training and testing, we found that the GBDT method was the best performer (see Table S7). Figure S10 presents the importance of covariates within the training samples as identified by the GBDT.

Modelling of carbon balance
To quantify the temporal trend of major carbon pools under the impact of the 2008 Wenchuan Earthquake, our carbon balance model adopts a pool–flux structure, employing a set of differential equations to simplify the connection between carbon flux and mass movements. We derived the parameters for the carbon balance model by integrating subsequent research and data collected since the Wenchuan event (particularly the carbon stock distribution maps obtained from empirical data noted above). This approach ensures that the parameter settings are tailored to our study area and effectively reflect complex environmental interactions. The carbon balance modelling separates into three main parts: constructing the carbon balance framework, introducing earthquake-triggered landslides and implementing carbon balance model. The model is based on two key assumptions: (1) following the earthquake, the entire aboveground biomass carbon pool (B) is converted into debris (D) that is fully mixed with soil carbon and buried within landslide deposits. Because this exact initial B–D portioning lacks empirical constraint, it represents a source of uncertainty in the estimated long-term carbon storage. This assumption represents an endmember maximum potential carbon storage after the earthquake; (2) ecosystems outside the landslide surface areas are assumed to have remained undisturbed, regions showing no bare surfaces or vegetation loss are assumed to have the same stock before and after the earthquake. The major carbon pools and fluxes are shown in Fig. S11.

Statistical analyses
For our field data, descriptive statistical analyses were conducted to characterise the spatial variations of soil organic carbon (SOC) content, soil total nitrogen (TN) content, and soil OC stock with depth, as well as tree, understory, litter, and total ecosystem organic carbon stocks in both undisturbed areas and landslide deposits (Table S8). Prior to model training, multicollinearity among covariates was evaluated using Pearson correlation analysis (Fig. S12). For the modelling of carbon stock analysis, we applied the Shapiro–Wilk test to examine the representativeness and normality of twenty selected covariates (see Table S9). Subsequently, a one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA, F test) was used to test whether the effect of coseismic landslides on OC stock is distinguishable (p<0.05) when comparing undisturbed areas and landslide deposits (see Table S10).

Data availability
The data generated or analysed during this study are included in the paper, Supplementary Information and the Source Data 1. Source data are provided with this paper.

Code availability
The codes to produce the carbon balance model are available at https://github.com/liujie1408/carbon-dynamics-model

## Authors' Response to Round 1

Response to Reviewers
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
This study presents a novel quantification of earthquake-induced terrestrial organic
carbon (OC) dynamics using the 2008 Wenchuan Earthquake as a case study. By
integrating field data, remote sensing, and numerical modelling, the authors present a
comprehensive carbon mass balance that accounts for storage, loss, and transport of OC
during and after the earthquake-induced sediment cascade. This work bridges tectonics
and the carbon cycle, offering a fresh perspective on seismic events as net carbon sinks
over millennial timescales.
We thank the reviewer for taking the time to read and provide very constructive comments on our
manuscript. We appreciate that the reviewer recognises the value of this high-quality and original
dataset. We have provided responses below to the general concerns and line-by-line changes.
However, some issues remain that require further clarification and explanation by the
authors before publication.
1. L56-57: What is the empirical basis for the claim that landslide deposits can remain
stable for “hundreds or even thousands of years,” given the dynamic nature of
mountainous terrain and climate variability?
There is strong empirical evidence demonstrating that landslide deposits can persist for centuries
to millennia, even within highly dynamic mountain environments. We have revised the the
paragraph starting at line 56 to more strongly identify the evidence. It now reads as follows:
“The largest continental earthquakes generate up to ~ 50 km3 of landslide deposits, which are
composed of a mixture of soil and fragmented rock (10). Landslides mix soil OC and live biomass
into these deposits, creating an OC store whose magnitude over time depends on the volume of
landslide deposits and the rate at which they are eroded (11). These deposits largely rest on
hillslopes, where typically less than 10% of these deposits are eroded immediately after the
earthquake, while the majority of deposits remain stable for hundreds or even thousands of years
(12-16). The rate of sediment and OC export is a function of the density of the newly developed
drainage network on the landslide itself together with its connectivity to the river below (17, 18)
and the efficiency of hillslope erosion processes such as debris flow generation (Francis). Where
this connectivity has been measured, for instance following the Chi-Chi, Wenchuan and Gorkha
earthquakes, 5–60% of landslides are shown to be connected to a drainage network (19), though
erosion is likely to be less efficient in the smallest headwater channels (20). The highest post-
event sediment yields measured historically are reported from the 1970 Madang Earthquake
(Papua New Guinea), where up to 50% of the mobilised sediment was exported in the first year
(21). And yet, much lower yields are more typical, such as in the Matiri River (New Zealand),
where at least 50–75% of the sediment generated by the 1929 Murchison Earthquake remained in
the catchment 50 years later (13). Evacuation of the 1999 Chi-Chi Earthquake debris filling the
Peikang River is predicted to take centuries (18, 22), just as 70% still remains intact of the 5–7
km3 of sediment injected into the Pokhara Valley (Nepal) by medieval earthquakes (23).”
2. L62-70: Why do some earthquake-induced landslide deposits remain stable for
centuries while others are rapidly evacuated?
Thank you very much for this insightful question. We have revised and clarified the current
understanding of this process in the paragraph starting on line 56, noting that it is still and open
question.
3. The “capacitor effect” is not clearly defined, which could mislead readers. Should
“capacitor” be defined earlier for broader accessibility?
Thank you for this helpful comment. We agree that the term “capacitor effect” required a clearer
and earlier definition for broader accessibility, as introducing it later in the manuscript could
potentially mislead readers. In response, we have revised the Introduction at Lines 48–51 to
explicitly define this concept. We now clarify that the volume of carbon temporarily stored in
landslide deposits, and the timescale over which it is subsequently released and exported,
effectively act as a “carbon capacitor”, buffering the interval between carbon production and its
eventual downstream transfer. Meanwhile, we then emphasized the carbon capacitor in the
statement of hypotheses at Line 105.
4. L130-131: Why recovery rates differ by 100x between landslide surfaces and overall
affected area?
The difference in recovery rates reflects how we have averaged the data, with one estimate based
on the entire affected area and the other is limited to the landslide surfaces. To clarify this point,
we have revised the text at Lines 174-176 to read: “…475±110 Mg C km-2 y--1 on landslide
surfaces and 5.5±0.02 Mg C km-2 yr-1 when applied to the overall affected area, reflecting that
landslides account for only about 8% of the total landscape area.”
5. L133–135: This reports no clear change in soil carbon content with depth in landslide
deposits. Was this finding consistent across all landslide types and locations, or are there
exceptions that should be discussed?
Our statement that soil carbon content with depth in landslides shows no clear trend immediately
following the earthquake was based on limited field observations. These field samples were taken
only to a depth of 50 cm, as illustrated in the Supplementary Material (Fig. S4). We acknowledge
that this limited dataset is not representative across all landslide types and locations, and we
currently lack sufficient information to generalize this trend. To avoid potential confusion for
readers, we have therefore removed the description at Line 178: “Our excavated soil profiles
show no clear change in carbon content with depth, suggesting vertical mixing for landslide
deposits”. We provide Fig.S4 and Fig.S5 showing the soil organic carbon stock and soil organic
carbon content changing trend in the Supplementary Materials, but we do not think it requires
further discussion in the main text.
6. L136–143: Could the authors quantify or elaborate more on the planted vs. natural
regrowth proportions?
We agree that quantifying the proportions of planted versus naturally regenerated vegetation
would be valuable for understanding post-landslide recovery. However, distinguishing these
proportions was not the main focus of our study, which primarily aimed to quantify the carbon
mass balance associated with earthquake-induced landslides and post-seismic sediment dynamics.
Vegetation recovery was considered mainly in terms of its contribution to post-earthquake carbon
storage, rather than as an ecological succession process.
In our field surveys, we found that only three landslide sites showed possible influence from
locally dispersed crop or tree seeds associated with nearby villages. Given the limited occurrence
and our focus on the carbon cycle rather than on vegetation origin, we removed the following
sentence (Line 183) to avoid overinterpretation: “Some of these new species are distinguished by
their rapid growth rates and resilient capacity for colonizing disturbed sites, while others
especially those of economic importance may have been planted as part of conservation policies
and projects in southwest China, rather than resulting from natural regrowth”.
7. L154-156: Would briefly noting potential reasons for the NPP vs. measured OC
discrepancy?
We have revised the text to clarify the relationship between NPP-derived and field-measured
organic carbon (OC). The field measurement represents the total OC stored in soil and vegetation
biomass, while NPP refers to the amount of OC fixed by plant photosynthesis minus plant
respiration losses. Given their different definitions and timescales, they are not directly
comparable. The observed ~10% lower field-measured OC compared to the NPP-derived estimate
is within the typical range of measurement uncertainty (Turner et al., 2005); however, it may also
reflect real carbon losses through fluvial transport, decomposition, and soil respiration.
Accordingly, the previous sentences in the manuscript has been revised at Lines 199-202: “The
field-measured OC represents the combined carbon storage in soil and vegetation biomass. The
measured OC was about 10% lower than the NPP-derived estimate, reflecting carbon losses
through fluvial transport, decomposition, and soil respiration. The field-measured OC represents
the combined carbon storage in soil and vegetation biomass. The measured OC was about 10%
lower than the NPP-derived estimate, which could partly reflect measurement uncertainty , in
addition to potential carbon losses through fluvial transport, decomposition, and soil
respiration.”
8. L353–362: Twenty covariates were used for machine learning. Please clarify whether
predictor importance or multicollinearity was evaluated, and whether any variables were
removed due to redundancy.
We have clarified in the revised Methods section that multicollinearity among covariates was
evaluated prior to model training. Specifically, we computed Pearson correlation matrices and
generated pairwise correlation plots for field sampling data across undisturbed areas (UD) and
landslide deposits (LD) in Fig. S12. In addition, both univariate and multivariate regression
analyses were performed to assess the relationships between each covariate and total organic
carbon (TOC).
During model training, variable importance was further evaluated based on the GBDT algorithm,
as illustrated in Figure S10. Nearly all initially selected covariates were retained, as they
represent distinct topographic, climatic, soil, and vegetation attributes and contribute
meaningfully to model performance. Although redundancy removal is often recommended in large
datasets, our relatively short dataset favored maintaining these representative covariates to avoid
overfitting while preserving interpretability and ensuring robust prediction accuracy.
Accordingly, we have modifed and added the following clarification to the Methods section at
Lines 510-520.
9. Supplementary Information: Was the normal distribution assumption for Monte Carlo
validated?
In the original submission, the uncertainty analysis was based on a deterministic propagation of
uncertainty, where bothα and γ were assumed to follow normal distributions as reported in
previous studies (Guzzetti et al., 2009; Larsen et al., 2010; Parker et al., 2011). The reviewer
correctly noted that this assumption was not explicitly validated in the earlier version.
In the revised manuscript (Lines 45-66 of Supplementary Note), we have replaced the analytical
approach with a Monte Carlo simulation framework, where α and γ are treated as normally
distributed variables following the same empirical parameterizations. The resulting ensemble of
total volumes allows us to characterize the output distribution directly. To provide a more
distribution-independent representation of uncertainty, we now report the interquartile range
(25th–75th percentiles) rather than the standard deviation. This modification effectively relaxes
the requirement for normally distributed inputs and outputs and makes the uncertainty
quantification more robust. We note that there has not been a significant change in our estimates
of uncertainty with this new method.
10. Supplementary Information: The authors apply both Marc et al. and Li et al. correction
methods for scar area estimation. Could they clarify how the choice between these
approaches affects the resulting landslide volume and the downstream carbon budget?
Applying the scale‐factor method of Li et al. (2014) generally yields larger scar areas—and
therefore greater total landslide volumes—than the geometry-based correction of Marc et al.
(2018). The difference arises because Li’s approach employs an empirical scale factor (fₛₐᵣ ≈ 0.70)
calibrated specifically for the Wenchuan inventory, whereas Marc’s method explicitly accounts
for the shape of each landslide polygon through its aspect ratio (K). Consequently, Li’s method
may overestimate scar areas when fₛₐᵣ is not regionally representative, while Marc’s approach
tends to reduce estimates for elongated or irregular landslides.
Given that volume scales nonlinearly with area (𝑉 =𝛼𝐴 𝛾 with 𝛾 >1), even moderate
s
differences in scar area can amplify into substantial discrepancies in total volume. Considering
this sensitivity and the limited spatial resolution of the available Wenchuan landslide inventory,
we were required to use the area–volume scaling relationship to estimate landslide volumes.
Meanwhile, given that the correction parameters proposed by Li et al. (2014) were derived
primarily from the Longmenshan fault zone, we adopted their correction method to compute the
source areas, providing the most reasonable estimate of total landslide volume across the study
area.
We agree with the reviewer that the choice of correction method can propagate through the
carbon balance model by influencing the derived landslide volumes and, in turn, the downstream
carbon budget. However, our analysis indicates that while the two methods affect the magnitude
of carbon fluxes, they do not alter the qualitative trends or the overall direction of post-seismic
carbon system evolution. Thus, averaging the results from both correction schemes provides a
balanced and robust representation under current data constraints.
In addition, we have revised the Supplementary Materials section titled “Uncertainty of
Landslide Volume” (Line 45-73) to include a dedicated discussion clarifying the uncertainty and
the additional variability arising from different parameter settings and correction methods.
11. Supplementary Information: The estimation of total landslide volume pools multiple
published empirical parameters. How do the authors select which parameter sets to use
for the Wenchuan region?
In our study, we included several published parameter sets, comprising both locally derived
values from the Longmenshan region (Parker et al., 2011) and global or regional compilations
(Guzzetti et al., 2009; Larsen et al., 2010). This choice ensures both regional relevance and
comparability with previous work. As the different parameter sets yield slightly different total
landslide volumes (Table S11), we reported all results and then used their average as the
representative estimate for subsequent calculations of sediment mass and carbon budgets. This
approach avoids reliance on any single parameterization, reflects the uncertainty among
published values, and provides a robust basis for our conclusions.
12. OC recovery is compared to NPP using remote sensing. How do the authors account
for root biomass and belowground OC, which may be underestimated by NPP-based
approaches?
In our study, vegetation biomass and corresponding organic carbon (OC) were estimated using
species-specific allometric equations compiled for Chinese forest types (see Lines 414–417 in the
Methods section). These equations explicitly include both above-ground and below-ground
components, thereby accounting for root biomass and belowground OC in the total vegetation
carbon stock. For species without specific equations, we used generalized allometric relationships
according to plant functional type (e.g., deciduous broad-leaved or evergreen broad-leaved
forests).
Therefore, root and belowground carbon were fully considered in our field-based OC estimates.
The remote-sensing–derived NPP data were used only to evaluate the temporal recovery trends of
vegetation productivity following the earthquake, not as a direct measure of total carbon storage.
So we clarified in manuscript at Lines 189-190:”..NPP was used solely to assess the temporal
recovery of vegetation productivity, not as a direct measure of total carbon storage.”
13. The carbon balance model pools all disturbance-derived carbon into three pools (B,
D, S). How sensitive are the model’s long-term predictions to the initial partitioning of
carbon among these pools, and what empirical data constrain these choices?
We are not aware of any empirical evidence that provides guidance on how to partition carbon
between these three pools after an earthquake or landslide. Consistent with our broader goal of
contrainin the upper bounds of carbon storage by an earthquake, we assume that after an
earthquake all of the B pool in areas where landslides occurs becomes the D pool. We have
updated the wording to note that this is a maximum estimate. Hence, following a landslide, the
biomass carbon (B pool) on affected slopes is entirely transferred to the buried debris (D pool),
while the soil carbon(S pool) retains its total mass but undergoes changes in density and spatial
distribution.
As noted in the Supplementary Note section “Modelling of Carbon Balance” (Lines 144–289),
the initial partitioning of carbon among the three pools following landslides is described in the
model equations. However, we agree that this assumption required clearer explanation.
Therefore, we have revised the text and added the following clarification at Lines 249–253 in
the Supplementary Materials: “…This setting represents an end-member assumption in which the
B pool is instantaneously converted to the D pool after landslides, corresponding to a 100%
transfer of B to D. This approach provides a maximum estimate of post-seismic carbon
redistribution, as no empirical data are currently available to constrain the actual B–D
conversion ratio.”

We thank the reviewer for this helpful suggestion. We have carefully reviewed the entire
manuscript to ensure that all abbreviations are defined at their first appearance. Specifically, net
primary productivity (NPP) is now defined at Line 169, and total nitrogen (TN) is defined at
Line 179. Similar adjustments have been made for other abbreviations where necessary to
improve clarity and consistency throughout the text.

We sincerely thank the reviewer for their positive and encouraging comments. Below we provide a

A general comment:
There is a large amount of additional information in the supplementary materials, some of

We agree that several important details were previously confined to the Supplementary

directly complements the corresponding sections of the manuscript.
Main points:
In summary, landslide volume is a key parameter in determining the amount of OC
mobilised, buried and stored, and eventually released, making it central to the study's
carbon budget calculations.
The estimates of landslide volume will, therefore, significantly impact the calculation of
the mobilised and buried organic carbon (OC), because landslide volume determines the
amount of soil and vegetation mobilised and buried, which directly correlates with the OC
mobilized and stored.
As the paper currently stands, I don’t believe there is enough discussion on how the
landslide source volumes have been derived and their uncertainties estimated, and what

We have revised the Supplementary Materials to make the derivation of landslide source volumes
and their uncertainties clearer and more traceable. Specifically, Lines 23–73 of the revised

(ii) explain the conversion from source area to volume using the adopted area–volume scaling,

Regarding the hypotheses, we made several modifications to the manuscript to clarify their

We then emphasized the carbon capacitor in the statement of hypotheses at Line 105. In addition,
we elaborated on the assumptions underlying the carbon balance model at Lines 498–508,
specifying that the biomass carbon pool (B) is assumed to be entirely converted into the debris
carbon pool (D) to represent the maximum potential carbon storage following the earthquake. A
brief explanation of this rationale is also provided in the main text at Lines 116–119. These

Regarding landslide types, we note that for the 2008 Wenchuan Earthquake there are 5

separates landslides by type or distinguishes source vs. deposit polygons at the level needed for

for the entire inventory. We have clarified this constraint and rationale in the Supplementary
(Lines 40–44) and cross-referenced it in the Methods (Lines 390-399).

Accurate landslide volume estimates are critical for modelling OC budgets. The study
uses volume-area scaling methods to convert landslide ‘area’ inventories into volume
estimates, which are then used to calculate OC stocks.
Recent work by Jones et al. (2024), highlights the limitations of existing landslide volume-

provides an important discussion on the limitations of existing volume–area scaling relationships.
In the revised manuscript, we have clarified the definition and terminology related to landslide
area. Specifically, throughout the main text and Supplementary Materials, we now consistently
use the term “landslide source area” to refer to the portion of the slope where material is initially
mobilized, and we have removed any ambiguous references to “scar area”. We use the term
“landslide surface” to refer to the denuded surface after landsliding, which included the source,
runout, and deposit zones.

Methods (Lines 390–399). Although we applied the empirical power-law volume–area
relationship to estimate landslide volumes, we corrected the mapped areas using the method
proposed by Li et al. (2016) to better represent the source area and reduce potential
overestimation. We also acknowledge, as noted by Jones et al. (2025), that such empirical scaling
may still lead to systematic underestimation of the true landslide volume when large and deep-
seated failures dominate the inventory.

not provide a consistent separation of source and deposit polygons, the adopted correction
remains the most reliable and regionally calibrated approach available. We have now added a
reference to Jones et al. (2025) and discussed this limitation and its potential effect on volume and
OC estimation in the revised manuscript and Supplementary Materials to make this uncertainty
explicit.
• The volume-area scaling relationships used and how these relate to different landslide
types in different materials – these have huge uncertainties associated with them. Would
incorporating other uncertainties adopting different methods of volume estimation (as per
those shown by Jones et al. 2025) impact the results?
We appreciate the reviewer’s valuable comment. We fully agree that large uncertainties are
inherent in landslide volume estimation due to the variability in scaling relationships and the
diversity of landslide types and materials. As discussed in our previous responses, our current
approach represents the most reliable and regionally calibrated method available given the
limitations of existing inventories for the Wenchuan Earthquake, which do not provide consistent
type or material classifications.
We acknowledge that incorporating alternative volume estimation methods, such as those
presented by Jones et al. (2025)), and accounting for landslide typologies (shallow and deep-
seated) through typology-specific volume-scaling relationships could more effectively constrain
these uncertainties and improve future carbon budget estimates. We plan to incorporate such
approaches in future work, particularly by applying higher-resolution models at the catchment
scale to better quantify and propagate the uncertainties associated with landslide volume
estimation.
• Why use landslide volume, what about using the landslide ‘scar’ area (which is less
uncertain) – noting the difference between source and scar – to calculate soil OC and live

landslide scar area provide a better estimate of removed and buried OC?
We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. As discussed above, we have unified the
terminology of landslide scar area and landslide source area throughout the manuscript and
Supplementary Materials. The landslide source area represents the primary input to the sediment
budget, while landslide volume is used in our carbon cycle model mainly to approximate the
initial sediment thickness that governs soil (S) and debris (D) export. Although incorporating soil
depth and vegetation type could, in principle, refine local estimates of OC loss and burial, soil
depth are not available at the regional scale. Therefore, in this study, we first fixed the soil depth
when calculating field-based OC stock distributions. In the carbon cycle model, we adopted a
volume-based approach and incorporated sediment transport processes as a consistent and
parsimonious means of representing carbon transfer across the study area..
These uncertainties and their impact on the estimated OC generated and stored by
coseismic landslides, could be used to address whether there is too much ‘noise’ versus
‘signal’ in the estimates, to be able to substantiate the studies initial hypotheses.
Currently I can’t tell.
We thank the reviewer for this valuable comment. We agree that incorporating multiple layers of
uncertainty could, in principle, introduce significant variability into the results. However, as
shown in Fig. 4, the overall impact remains limited, and even under extreme parameter settings,
the model outcomes do not deviate substantially from the mean estimates. This stability arises
because the uncertainties associated with landslide volume estimation are effectively moderated
through the formulation of h(t) in our carbon cycle model (Supplementary Note), which constrains
their propagation into the pool dynamics. Consequently, while uncertainty inevitably exists, the
modelled signal remains strong enough to substantiate the study’s initial hypotheses.
In addition, the Wenchuan EQ is thought to be an outlier wrt., the number and area
affected by coseismic landslides. Is it therefore, representative of other EQ events and
the landslides and OC they generate and store? Wenchuan could be
anomalous wrt., number of landslides generated, but was less OC mobilised and buried in the area (per
unit area of landslide scar?) when compared to the landslides triggered in other recent
coseismic events (listed) thus making it less anomalous? How does this anomalous
event support the studies hypotheses?
We thank the reviewer for this valuable comment. The Wenchuan Earthquake represents one of
the largest and well-documented events associated with widespread coseismic landsliding. In this
study, we assume that all mobilized organic carbon is immediately buried within landslide
deposits, allowing us to quantify the maximum potential carbon “capacitor effect” of such a
mega-earthquake. This does not imply that a larger number or total area of landslides necessarily
leads to higher carbon mobilization, as the primary OC stock density also plays a critical role. In
this context, the Wenchuan event supports our first hypothesis—that worldwide variations in
carbon export reflect differences in the primary mass of OC mobilised during earthquakes.
Although the Wenchuan earthquake generated an exceptionally large number of landslides, the
amount of OC mobilized and subsequently buried per unit area is comparable to, or even lower
than, in some other seismically active regions, like in Southern Alps. This highlights that carbon
response is controlled not only by the extent of landslides disturbance but also by fluvial systems,
topographic and climatic factors. The carbon cycle model we developed further aims to capture
these dependencies, allowing us to explore both the intensity and timescale of post-seismic carbon
recovery.

OC Mobilisation:

other landslide events. However, the Wenchuan EQ and the landslides it generated are
reported to be an outlier wrt., to other EQ events and the landslides they generated?
Please discuss this in more detail.

on the total amount of organic carbon mobilised, transported, and subsequently recovered across
different earthquake-induced landslide events. These estimates vary among studies because of
differences in measurement approaches, data sources, and observation timescales. Moreover,
several factors—including primary productivity, microbial respiration, sediment yield, and fluvial
transport capacity—can substantially influence the magnitude of observed OC mobilisation and
accumulation.

Southern Alps partly reflects the use of lake sediment records that integrate carbon accumulation

other reported events. To clarify this point, we have revised the text at Lines 289–292 and
updated the Table 1 caption to better highlight these distinctions.

magnitude of OC mobilised depends on the initial coseismic landslide volume and any
entrainment of additional debris as the landslide mass moves downslope and buried by

broken down due to movement? Some commentary on the importance of landslide type and OC
